name: arturo
desc: Simple, modern and portable programming language for efficient scripting
why: A modern, unusual scripting language with a distinctive design, worth a look for language enthusiasts.

brief.what_it_is: Arturo is an independently developed, modern, general-purpose scripting language, written in Nim, that runs on a bytecode VM. Scripts are plain text files run with the arturo executable. The README's sample is a recursive factorial function plus a loop that prints results, showing the syntax. The homepage says it ships a built-in web server, UI toolkit, databases, cryptography, HTTP clients and templating, and that scripts can be bundled into standalone executables. The homepage lists Linux, macOS, Windows and FreeBSD, plus a JS web build.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says the language is 'vaguely related to various other ones' including Logo, Rebol, Forth, Ruby, Haskell, D, Smalltalk, Tcl and Lisp, and the homepage pitches it as 'The Swiss Army Knife for ultra-efficient coding'. The author named it after a pet Emperor Scorpion, a quiet and docile creature, as a hint at what the language aspires to be.
brief.how_it_works: The README's core principles are that code is just a list of words, symbols and literal values, and that words and symbols within a block are interpreted according to context. There are no reserved words or keywords. The homepage says the language has an optimized bytecode VM with no warm-up or compilation step before a script runs.

commands_seen.context: Installs the most recent stable Arturo on Unix or macOS, per the README and homepage.
Installs the nightly (most recent) build instead of the stable release.
Homebrew install on macOS. The README warns the Homebrew version may not be the latest.
Starts the official Docker image for a quick taste of the language. The README says it is not meant for everyday use.
Runs a local script inside the Docker container by mounting the current directory at /home.

brief.install_notes: Pre-built binaries exist for practically all OSes, so the README says there is no real install step: download a binary and run it. The alternative is the curl installer above. The homepage says the installer supports Linux, macOS, FreeBSD and Windows through WSL, Git Bash or MSYS2. Nightly builds are on a separate nightlies repo. Manual builds are described on the GitHub wiki under Building Arturo. No accounts or runtimes are mentioned.
brief.standout: The 'no reserved words' design, where code is a list of words and symbols interpreted by context, is unusual among scripting languages, and the README invites users to redefine operators and build domain-specific languages. The Rebol-style block model is a distinctive choice, and it ships its own bundling and a wide built-in standard library.
brief.status: Appears maintained. The homepage lists official release 0.10.0 'Arizona Bark', and the MIT copyright runs to 2019-2026. The README has a live CI badge and an activity graph, and points to a nightly builds repo. I did not find an exact date for the last release or commit, so this is a lean, not a confirmed date.
brief.caveats: The README says the Docker image 'won't cut it' for everyday compiler use. The Homebrew formula may lag the latest version, and the README advises the pre-built binaries as the safer option. The README says the language is 'independently developed' and maintained by a small group in their spare time. The homepage claims a web build but only lists a MINI build for it. The language is young, and the README and homepage describe it as 'vaguely related' to many older languages with no formal spec mentioned.
quotes: Code is just a list of words, symbols and literal values
No reserved words or keywords - look for them as hard as you can; there are absolutely none
Simple, expressive & portable programming language for efficient scripting
fetch_log: https://arturo-lang.io/ - worked, but it is a marketing page with no README content; it gave the tagline, feature list, install curl line and release 0.10.0.
https://github.com/arturo-lang/arturo - worked, returned the README. I guessed this URL from the homepage's GitHub button, since the link target was not visible in the fetched text.

judge.reason: Its Rebol-style blocks and context-dependent words, with no reserved keywords, make Arturo an intriguing language-design rabbit hole rather than just another scripting runtime.

entry.title: Arturo
entry.tldr: A small scripting language with no reserved words, where code is just a list of words and symbols read by context, descended from Rebol, Forth and Lisp.
entry.deeper_look:
Arturo is an independently developed scripting language written in Nim. Scripts are plain text files, run with the `arturo` executable on a bytecode VM that the homepage says has no warm-up or compilation step. The homepage also lists a built-in web server, UI toolkit, databases, cryptography, HTTP clients and templating, and says scripts can be bundled into standalone executables.

The README says it is 'vaguely related to various other ones', naming Logo, Rebol, Forth, Ruby, Haskell, D, Smalltalk, Tcl and Lisp. The author named it after a pet Emperor Scorpion, a quiet and docile creature, as a hint at what the language aims to be.

The idea underneath is the one worth poking at. The README puts it this way: 'Code is just a list of words, symbols and literal values.' Words and symbols in a block are interpreted according to context, and there are no keywords at all. The README's challenge is to 'look for them as hard as you can; there are absolutely none'. That Rebol-style block model is what lets you redefine operators and build small domain-specific languages inside the language itself.

It is a good door into how a language can be built from very few parts, and into what a language looks like when its syntax is mostly data.
entry.install:
brew install arturo
# The README warns the Homebrew version may lag behind; pre-built binaries or the installer are the safer route:
# curl -sSL https://get.arturo-lang.io | sh

try_this.what_happens: Lists the options the executable accepts, a first look at how scripts are run.
Starts the official Docker image for a quick taste without installing anything. The README says it is not meant for everyday use.
Installs the nightly build instead of the stable release.

entry.whats_unique: Most scripting languages reserve keywords. Arturo has none, so code is a list of words interpreted by context, and you can redefine operators and build your own DSLs. It also ships a wide standard library and its own bundling.
entry.caveats: The language is young and maintained by a small group in their spare time, and the Homebrew formula may lag the latest release.
